1:
Henry treats the case as singular, thinking no like case occurred at that time in all Israel, and supposes the personal character of the women added weight to the plea. He describes the court in English terms, Moses sitting as king, the princes as lords, and the elders as their commons, and observes that the assembly sat near the tabernacle door so that the oracle might be consulted. Gill has them coming to what the Targum of Jonathan calls the house of judgment, and gives the anxiety that brought them, that the land was to be divided among those numbered, and only males of twenty years and upward were. Clarke says simply that the singular case of these women caused an additional law to be made. Keil notes that Moses brought the question of right before God, and that further directions about the marriage of heiresses were added later in the book.

Calvin alone stands back to ask what the ruling settles. Since the law gives no name to women, he says, it would seem no account of them was to be taken in the division of the land, and God did lay this down as the general rule; what follows is a special exception, made whenever a family is destitute of male heirs, for the preservation of the name. He then does something the others do not, and concedes the difficulty: he is aware that the point is open to dispute, and rests only on the decree God pronounced. He is generous about the motive too: although the daughters plead for their own advantage, the discussion arose from a good principle, since they would never have been so anxious if God's promise had not been to them as certain as if they already held the land.

The plea itself Calvin examines most closely. Its restriction in time aided their cause, since carrying the question back to an earlier period might have originated many quarrels; and by denying that their father was in the company of Korah they exclude the crimes whose punishment fell upon the posterity of the criminals, so that his private sin stands contrasted with public ignominy. On what that private sin was he is blunt: it is mere childish nonsense, he says, for the Jews to affirm that Zelophehad was the man who gathered sticks on the sabbath day, or one of the number of those who were slain. His editor supplies the gloss Calvin is refusing, that Jarchi reports Rabbi Akiba for the wood-gathering and Rabbi Simeon for the contumacious company. Wesley takes the phrase at its face and adds the belief behind it, that the words mean his own personal sins, and that it was a truth believed by the Jews that death was a punishment for a man's own sins.

How the name was to be preserved is disputed three ways, and Gill sets out all of them. The Targum of Jonathan, with which Jarchi agrees, makes their motion a request that their mother might marry their father's brother under the levirate law; Gill objects that it does not appear that law was yet in being, while admitting he cannot easily say how else the name would be preserved. The second reading, which he reports and Wesley says some gather, is that the first son of each heiress was called after Zelophehad or after Hepher, by virtue of the law which made a brother's first son bear the name of the elder brother whose widow he married. The third is the plainest and Gill thinks it confirmed by what follows, that the Jews commonly understand by the name no other thing than the inheritance itself. Wesley closes on the confidence of the request, that they asked a possession in a land not yet conquered, concluding it certainly would be, and thereby gave glory to God.
5:
Why the cause went up to God at all is answered two ways. Gill takes it as jurisdiction, that the question was too difficult for the court and devolved upon Moses as its president, he alone having recourse to God at all times; and he adds the rabbinic frame, that the Targums count this one of four causes which came before Moses and which he solved according to the mind of the Lord, the others being the blasphemer, those defiled by the dead, and the sabbath breaker. Calvin supposes rather that the judges were divided, or in doubt about an obscure point, and holds it expedient that the rule be laid down by God so that no future controversy might arise, a human sentence perhaps not setting the obstinacy of many at rest. What he chiefly wants noticed is the bearing of the man: it is worth remarking, he says, the pious modesty of Moses, who was not ashamed to confess his ignorance until he had been instructed by the mouth of God, and who, though he had promulgated the law forty years before, was still always ready to learn. From which he draws the lesson that rulers ought to have recourse to God in points of perplexity, though he no longer answers from heaven.

The masculine pronoun in the grant is the curiosity of the passage, and it is Clarke who insists on it. There is an anomaly in the Hebrew, he says, invisible in our translation, since the masculine forms are used of the daughters where the feminine were to be expected, the words for them and for their father both standing in the masculine though governed by the noun for daughters. He then reports what others have made of it, with visible reserve, remarking that interpreters have sought a hidden meaning here and have found several, whether hidden here or not: that the masculine is used because these daughters are treated as if they were heirs male; that it is on account of their faith and their conscientious regard to ancient custom and to keeping their father's memory in being, which might well benefit men; and that it signifies the free gift of God. Ellicott states the difficulty in two lines and offers a fourth possibility that Clarke does not report, that the reference may be to the sons of Zelophehad's daughters, before allowing the alternative that the daughters must simply be regarded in the light of sons.

On the general law that follows, the commentators divide the labour rather than disagree. Keil sets out the whole order of succession, that where a man leaves no son the landed property passes to his daughters, in default of daughters to his brothers, then to his paternal uncles, and failing those to his next of kin, and refers the reader to his own antiquities and to Selden's treatise. Ellicott, on the same verse, sends the reader to the same two authorities. Gill notes only that the affair occasioned a law in which all the people would have a concern.

Calvin is the one who asks how far the preference for daughters reaches. God prefers the daughters to all other relatives where there is no male issue, he says, but with that single exception at the first degree admits none but males, so preserving the usual order. He gives a reason on each side: it would be very unjust to exclude a man's own natural heirs on account of their sex, but once it became necessary to pass beyond his own children to other kindred, the prerogative of the male line began. And he limits the whole discussion expressly to the land of Canaan, in which not only the name of Abraham but the names of the twelve tribes were to be preserved, so that the memory of the blessing might be the more distinct and unclouded.
9:
The remainder of the succession is stated without dispute and glossed twice. Keil renders the closing phrase a statute determining right, and Wesley says the same in plainer terms, a rule by which the magistrates shall give judgment in such cases. Wesley also enters a small correction the text itself does not make: where the statute says brethren, sisters are to be understood as well, and he grounds it on the clause about daughters which stands a few verses earlier. Gill carries the chain down with a single addition at each step, that where brothers or uncles are named their descendants are included.

Ellicott sees something in the placing of the next command that nobody else remarks. Its standing in immediate connection with the answer returned to the daughters of Zelophehad is very remarkable: they were to enter the land of promise and their descendants to inherit it, while the great lawgiver himself was to be excluded for his transgression; and Moses does not shrink from recording the sentence in the very position that brings his exclusion into greater prominence. Henry stays with the fault rather than the arrangement, that God tells Moses of his speaking unadvisedly at the waters of strife, where he failed to express as carefully as he ought a regard to the honour both of God and of Israel; though a faithful servant and highly favoured, he shall hear of it, and all the world shall hear of it too, since God will show his displeasure against sin even in those nearest and dearest to him. From which Henry draws the warning that those in reputation for wisdom and honour have need to be constantly careful of their words and ways, lest they say or do what may be a diminution to their comfort or their credit a great while after.

On the mountain itself the three who describe it do not agree. Clarke identifies it flatly as Nebo, which he takes to be the same as Pisgah, and adds Dr Shaw's description of the range as a long ridge of frightful, rocky, precipitous hills continued all along the eastern coast of the Dead Sea as far as the eye can reach; he derives the name from the verb to pass over, so that Abarim signifies passages, the ridge being named from the passage of the Israelites opposite it. Wesley arranges the same three names differently, making Abarim the whole tract, Nebo one of its highest points, and Pisgah the top of Nebo. Ellicott arranges them differently again, making the mountains of Abarim the Moabitish table-land whose northern portion bore the name Pisgah, and observing that Nebo is sometimes described as one of the mountains of Abarim and at other times as the top of Pisgah. Gill notes only what the seeing amounted to, that Moses was admitted to look and no more, entrance being denied him though he importuned for it.

What it is to be gathered to one's people is put once negatively and once positively. Ellicott rules out one reading, that in the case of Moses, as in that of Abraham, the expression cannot be understood with reference to the place of burial. Wesley supplies the positive sense: Moses must die, but death does not cut him off, it only gathers him to his people and brings him to rest with the patriarchs who went before, since Abraham and Isaac and Jacob were his people, the people of his choice, and to them death gathered him. Keil observes what the announcement was for, that it was made so that Moses might go forward to his death knowing what lay before him, and that it was this announcement which moved him to ask that a leader be appointed lest the congregation be as a flock without a shepherd.
15:
What the prayer shows about the man is what all of them want to say. Henry sets it against the alternative: when the reprieve Moses had solicited could not be obtained, he begged that the work of God might be carried on though he himself should not have the honour of finishing it, and adds the sentence that fixes it, that envious spirits do not love their successors and Moses was not one of these. Calvin calls the affection paternal, since Moses not only shunned no pains to the end of his life but made provision for the time after it, anxious that the people should not be left like a headless body. Ellicott makes him a type of one greater, whose word was that they should weep not for him but for themselves and their children, since instead of indulging grief or unavailing remorse his mind was fixed on the welfare of those for whose sake he had once been willing that his own name should be blotted out of the book. Wesley's comment here is Henry's own almost word for word, that we should concern ourselves in our prayers and endeavours for the rising generation, that God's kingdom may be advanced when we are in our graves.

Why he asked rather than appointed is answered twice, and the two answers are not the same. Calvin makes it humility about a competence he actually possessed: Moses neither arrogates the right of appointment to himself nor on his own authority submits it to the election of the people, but establishes God as sole arbiter; it was permitted him to choose officers, that being part of the political constitution, but this task was too difficult for man's judgment, so the power had to be entrusted to God alone. Ellicott makes it self-denial about a preference he might have indulged, that instead of appointing one of his own family or the man of his own choosing he commits the matter to God and prays for one who would be a true shepherd.

The title given to God in the prayer is weighted differently by the two who expound it. Gill presses the second half, that the souls of men are called the spirits of all flesh, that is of corporeal beings, precisely to distinguish them from the angels, who though spirits are incorporeal; and the God who made them knows their capacities and fitness for service. Wesley presses the first half, that this is the searcher of spirits, who knows who is fit for the employment, and the giver and governor of spirits, who can raise and suit the spirits of men to the highest and hardest works. Keil denies that the spirit in the next verse means insight and wisdom, making it the higher power inspired by God into the soul, which quickens the moral and religious life.

The phrase about going out and coming in is given three different compasses. Gill offers three readings without choosing, that it means going before them in war and bringing them home in peace, or simply the administration of civil government, or something particular to leading Israel out of the wilderness into Canaan. Ellicott takes the first pair as a common idiom for the ordinary life of man and the second as the direction of the conduct of others, after the manner of a shepherd with his flock. Wesley explains the metaphor from practice, that shepherds in those countries did not walk behind their sheep as ours now do but before them, leading them out to pasture and in due time home again. Clarke fastens instead on what the image tells us about Moses, that it is a beautiful expression showing in what light he viewed himself: he was their shepherd, he sought no higher place, he fed and guided the flock of God under the direction of the Divine Spirit.
18:
What the spirit in Joshua is gets four answers, and they do not agree. Clarke will have it plainly, that this must certainly mean the Spirit of God, and turns it at once upon the ministry: how miserably qualified is that man for the work of God who is not guided and influenced by the Holy Ghost. Ellicott withholds that identification on grammatical grounds, noting that the definite article is not used in the original and that the word appears to denote spiritual endowment and qualification rather than the giver of it. Calvin agrees with Ellicott in substance and adds the observation neither of the others makes, that the word is used here in a different sense from the sense it bore two verses earlier: there it named the God of the spirits of all flesh, and here it stands by a common enough figure for the gifts that proceed from the Spirit, so that God is not merely intimating that Joshua has a soul but that he excels in the gifts the office needs, intelligence and judgment and magnanimity and skill in war. Wesley enumerates them in his own way, as the spirit of government, of wisdom, and of the fear of the Lord. Calvin also notices a fact he says is stated nowhere else, that Joshua was given in answer to the prayers of Moses.

Whether the laying on of hands conferred anything or only declared it is the sharper question. Ellicott argues that it conferred, and argues it from a later text: the spiritual qualifications of Joshua did not supersede the necessity of an outward consecration, and more than that, special qualifications seem to have been bestowed in connection with the imposition of the hands of Moses, since it is written that Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom for Moses had laid his hands upon him. Wesley takes both together, that by the ceremony Moses at once designed the person and conferred the power, and by the prayers which accompanied the rite obtained from God the spiritual gifts and graces necessary for the employment. Gill sets a limit against exactly this. What Moses was told to put upon Joshua, he says, was not the Spirit that was on Moses nor the gifts of the Spirit, since to do that is the Lord's work and not any man's, but the honour of civil government: a share in it, so that Joshua should be used no longer as a minister and servant, as he had been, but as colleague and partner, with some of the ensigns of power and some exercise of it. Calvin adds only that the rite was in use before the giving of the Law, the holy patriarchs having blessed in this manner,.

On the public setting of the man before the people there is no dispute at all. Gill says he was set before Eleazar and the congregation that they might be witnesses of what was said and done to him. Wesley says the same and adds what the charge was for, that Moses should give him counsels and instructions for the right management of so great a trust; Ellicott supplies the words of the charge from a later chapter, that he was to be strong and of a good courage. Keil sets the sequence out as the text gives it, the setting before the priest and the congregation, the charge given in their sight, and the honour put upon him that the congregation might be obedient. On that last clause Clarke reads the point as public association, that Moses was to show the whole congregation he had associated Joshua with himself in the government, and Wesley gives the reason of policy behind it, that the people, being used to obey him while Moses lived, might do it afterwards the more cheerfully.
21:
That Joshua must stand before the priest is read by two of them in opposite senses. Clarke takes it as a diminution and says so plainly: here was a remarkable difference between him and Moses, for God talked with Moses face to face, but spoke to Joshua only through the medium of the high priest. Calvin takes the same arrangement as a dignifying of the rule rather than a lowering of the ruler. Joshua is subordinated to the priest on one point only, to inquire of God by the Urim and Thummim, and the dignity of the priesthood is exalted by that symbol, since the prince consults God by the mouth of a man who, clothed in the sacred ephod, answers as the interpreter of God himself. From which Calvin draws the conclusion he wants: the passage shows that the rule of Joshua was not profane, since in all legitimate dominion religion ought to hold the first place, and it is absurd that things which depend wholly upon God should be separated from his service.

Gill contributes a piece of rabbinic protocol that nobody else has. The high priest, he reports, did not come into the king's presence except when he pleased, and did not stand before him; rather the king stood before the high priest, though the high priest was commanded to honour the king and to rise when he came. But the king does not stand before him except when consulting by the judgment of Urim, which is the case in hand. And Gill notices that the posture here is not the ordinary one: in consultation the priest stands with his face toward the ark and the enquirer stands behind him with his face to the priest's back, whereas Joshua is described as standing before the priest, as a king or supreme governor would. Wesley adds two smaller points, that Urim is put for both Urim and Thummim, and that the consulting was not constant but for such times as required it and for important and difficult matters; Ellicott states the obligation flatly, that Joshua and the children of Israel were to abide by the decision obtained through Urim and Thummim.

On the execution of the command Gill and Wesley make the same argument independently and Wesley makes it best. It had been little, he says, for Moses to resign his honour to a son of his own; but with his own hands to ordain Eleazar as high priest and now Joshua as chief ruler, while his own children had no preferment at all and were left in the rank of common Levites, was more to his glory than the highest advancement of his family could have been, and shows him to have had a principle which raised him above all other lawgivers. Gill puts the same facts to a different use, that this is clear proof Moses was no impostor, since he neither sought to aggrandise his family nor repined that the priesthood went to his brother's line and the civil government to his servant of the tribe of Ephraim. He adds Jarchi's observation that Moses did the thing cheerfully and did more than he was commanded, since the Lord said lay thine hand and he laid both his hands. Keil records only that he laid his hands upon him and gave him a charge as the Lord commanded.

Clarke ends the chapter by looking past it. The laying on of hands was proof that Joshua was appointed to the work and qualified for it, and at his word the people were to go out and come in; and in this Clarke sees him a type of our blessed Lord in his mediatorial office and in his divine appointment as man to the work of our salvation. Then he checks the comparison himself, that one infinitely greater than either Moses or Joshua is here.
